course_description:
The internship provides a range of opportunities for students to work with UQ-based, or affiliated, organisations and researchers, assisting with project-based work, event organisation, and editorial and publishing activities. Students will gain practical experience by working within professional organisations involved in literary and historical research, library resource management, writing and publishing, communications, and cultural heritage management. During the internship, students will critically engage with the internship through journal writing and a research-based essay; they may also contribute to other publications and scholarly outcomes.

To apply to enrol in this course:

Applications are decided on the basis of academic record and relevant background and are subject to availability of placements. We endeavour to give students one of their 3 top preferences however due to the limited number of places, competitive entry may apply to some options. Also note that some placement options require an interview with the placement provider.

This course will appeal to students interested in gaining practical professional experience in the fields of literary and historical studies, research communication and public engagement, professional writing, the publishing industry, library-based cultural heritage and conference management. Within the course’s general workload requirements and with the advice of their supervisors, students can gain practical, organisational, research, and publishing experience.

For the list of current placement options, email the course convenor . All internships are subject to availability. Students also have the option of organising their own placement with a suitable organisation, subject to permission from the course convenor and placements officer.

Employability Statement:

Studying English Literature develops advanced skills in written and oral communication, critical thinking, research, and cultural knowledge and understanding. Through close reading, discussion, writing, and independent research, students learn to analyse complex ideas, construct persuasive arguments, collaborate effectively, and engage thoughtfully with diverse perspectives and literary forms. These capabilities are highly valued across a wide range of professions, including education, government, media, publishing, law, healthcare, and the creative industries. Literary study also fosters adaptability, ethical reasoning, and the confidence to undertake long-term projects and communicate ideas clearly to different audiences. Students are encouraged to reflect on these skills throughout their degree and to recognise how literary study prepares them for diverse career pathways, an ability to engage in lifelong learning, and to be and to be responsible citizens in pluralistic societies.

In ENGL3020 you will develop skills relevant to your employability, including written and verbal communication skills, reflective practice and the ability to work independently and in teams on placement tasks and in the context of your cohort during course meetings. Practical experiences gained during the placements will constitute a valuable addition to your transferable skills and the development of your cv.

course_aims: The aim of the course is to give students professional experience in areas intersecting with the Arts and Cultural Heritage. Students have an opportunity to gain insights in to the ways that academic disciplines, including Professional Writing, Editing & Publishing; Literary Studies;ﾠGender Studies; and, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander studies, conduct, publish, and present professional research and scholarship, not only to academic communities, but also to a wider public. Students working on digital humanities projects such as with AustLit will also follow this same aim of facilitating the production and dissemination of academic research, sometimes undertaking original research, but also havingﾠthe opportunity to produce a scholarly outcome of their own. Those working in the Fryer library will gain experience in a range of preservation and information management strategies and techniques.ﾠStudents in the Writing, Editing and Publishing (WEP) program can use this course to gain practical experience in publishing and editing.ﾠ​

Word count: variable Task Instructions : The Management of Learning tasks comprise 3 components: · Completion of tasks set by the internship supervisor (20 marks) : This component involves liaising with the placement supervisor, proactively seeking out work, showing initiative for periods when there are no specific tasks set by the supervisor, completion of tasks, and reporting back to the supervisor. Students are expected to behave professionally at all times. If they are unable to attend the workplace for any reason, they must contact their supervisor to let them know and provide an explanation. The course coordinator will consult with students’ supervisors at the end of semester for allocating a mark for this component. · Active participation in meetings (10 marks) : Students are expected to attend and actively participate in the 5 course meetings (weeks 2, 5, 7, 9 and 12). Activities will include discussion of internship progress, small group work, and scaffolding tasks. · Peer review of scaffolding tasks for Placement Report Essay (10 marks) : This component involves bringing a draft abstract and a 1 page outline of the proposed report to the week 9 meeting and providing constructive feedback to peers on their draft abstracts and outlines. Criteria : Completion of tasks set by the internship supervisor in a timely way; organisational skills; a professional and courteous attitude to supervisors; and having a proactive attitude to the internship. (20 marks) Active participation in meetings. Students are expected to initiate discussion, engage with their peers, and share ideas and experiences. (10 marks) Peer review: providing constructive feedback in a collegial way on the draft abstracts and outlines of other students in the group (10 marks). assessment_details.task_description: Word count: 150 words each journal post plus 2 responses (1-2 sentences each) Task Instructions : Students will post weekly reflections on the internship and respond briefly to the posts of others . Upload a 150-word post each week (weeks 2-11), by Friday 4pm , to the Learn@UQ ENGL3020 course site padlet. The entries may, for example: record tasks, reflect on experiences and challenges, critically evaluate the aims and progress of the project, or reflect more broadly on the aims and methods of the type of work that the project represents and how it is situated within the humanities. In addition to uploading your own journal post, students are expected to respond briefly (1-2 sentences) to 2 posts from others each week. [Responses due by 4pm the following Monday.] Criteria : Journal posts: completion of 10 weekly posts (weeks 2-11) (approx. 150 words each) evidencing reflection on the internship (10 marks) Response (1-2 sentences) to the posts of others (2 per week) (5 marks) Open Assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Note that, while this assessment is classified as open assessment, journal posts are more likely to evidence genuine reflection if the task is not outsourced to AI. Also note that this task does not judge the quality of the writing but only whether the posts reflect genuine reflection. If AI/MT is used, it must be referenced in each post. assessment_details.title: Placement Report Essay
assessment_details.task_description: Word count : 1750 words, excluding Works Cited list. Task Instructions : The student will write a report in response to their internship experience. The report will comprise: · Abstract (250 words) providing an overview of the report. · Introduction (250 words) to the organisation/placement of their internship and its contexts within the humanities industry. · Tasks (250 words): an outline of the tasks and activities undertaken as part of the internship. · Reflection (500 words) on the placement experience, drawing from the journal entries and at least 1 secondary source on reflective practice. · Future directions (250 words): ideas on potential future projects for the organisation/placement, or suggested improvements to procedures or practices (eg on sustainability, inclusion, First Nations research methodology, community outreach, ethical practices etc). This section should include at least 1 secondary source relevant to your ideas or the contexts of your organisation/placement. · Transferable skills (250 words): an outline of your skills and abilities that you could include in your cv or for a job application. Style guide: MLA style. Criteria : Abstract providing concise and coherent overview of the report (5 marks) Clarity and coherence of report content (20 marks) Thoughtful reflection on the experiences of the internship and the project (10 marks) Writing mechanics and expression; presentation and MLA style (10 marks) Open Assessment: In this assessment you can use resources such as your notes, course materials, and other tools, including AI, while completing the task. The focus is not on memorising information, but on understanding, applying judgement, and demonstrating your own thinking. Note that: · while this assessment is classified as open assessment, so the use of AI is permissible, students should be aware that the use of AI may result in errors and fabricated information and sources. If the assessment submission contains fabricated materials, the submission may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct and will be submitted for integrity review. · If AI/MT is used, it must be acknowledged on the cover sheet and referenced in the Works Cited list. · Students should be capable of demonstrating detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools. Library Materials and Gen-AI : Students are also reminded that library materials may not be entered into AI technologies without express permission: Policies and guidelines - Library - The University of Queensland “You may not share, re-publish, copy or enter into AI technologies any part of a resource accessed from our online collections unless expressly permitted in the licence terms for that resource” “Except as permitted under each Publisher's terms and conditions of use, you must not: Use UQ Library resource content as an input to generative AI products or services” For referencing AI/MT see the Library guide: https://guides.library.uq.edu.au/referencing/ai-tools-assignments For referencing AI in MLA style see: How do I cite generative AI in MLA style? from the official MLA style website. policies_and_procedures: University policies and procedures apply to all aspects of student life. As a UQ student, you must comply with University-wide and program-specific requirements, including the: Student Code of Conduct Policy Student Integrity and Misconduct Policy and Procedure Assessment Procedure Examinations Procedure Reasonable Adjustments for Students Policy and Procedure AI for Assessment Guide Recording of Teaching Policy and Procedure Learn more about UQ policies on my.UQ and the Policy and Procedure Library . You'll also need to be aware of the following policies and procedures while completing this course: Placement Course guidelines Communication Expectations While you are a student at UQ, all communication must be conducted according to the UQ Student Code of Conduct . The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct. Emails like this will be reported to the University, and the matter will be pursued as misconduct. Learning activities
